## Запросы

q1:
I am designing the data model of an open-source Laravel "drive + collaborative documents" package (folders, binary files with content-addressed blobs, and rich-text documents edited with TipTap/ProseMirror + Yjs via a Hocuspocus hub). I want to align it with how mature systems do it: Google Drive API v3, Amazon S3 (versioning, lifecycle, Object Lock), Dropbox API, Box API, Microsoft Graph/OneDrive/SharePoint, Nextcloud. Please answer with concrete, documented behavior (cite official docs) and say clearly where something is undocumented. For each topic give: (a) what each system documents, (b) the common pattern, (c) a concrete recommendation for my package.

1. File vs native document aggregates. Google Drive distinguishes binary files (headRevisionId, md5Checksum, revisions with keepForever, revision download) from Google Docs (no binary content, export only, revisions not downloadable). How should a node table model "current content": one polymorphic current_version_id pointing either to a file revision or a document revision, or separate aggregates (files table with current file revision, documents table with current document revision) sharing a common node/metadata row? What do Drive, Box (file versions, "current version"), OneDrive (driveItem versions, file facet vs package facet) and Notion/Confluence do? Are revisions immutable once created? How is restore of an older revision done (copy-forward as a new head revision vs moving the pointer back)?

2. Deletion lifecycle. Document precisely: Drive trashed / explicitlyTrashed / auto-delete after 30 days / emptyTrash / permanent delete permissions; behaviour of children when a folder is trashed and restored; Box trash + retention policies + legal holds; Dropbox deleted files + restore + permanently_delete; OneDrive recycle bin (first/second stage); S3 delete markers, noncurrent version expiration, Object Lock retention modes (governance/compliance) and legal hold. What is the common state machine (active -> trashed -> purged, plus holds)? Is "archive" (read-only but not trashed) a distinct state anywhere (e.g. Box, Google Shared drives, Slack/Notion archive)? How do they handle purge of content that is still referenced elsewhere (dedup / shared blobs), and infected/quarantined files?

3. Optimistic concurrency and validators. Compare Drive (etag removed in v3? "version" field monotonically increasing for any change, headRevisionId for content), Box (etag / If-Match on file and folder operations, sequence_id), Dropbox (rev, update mode), S3 (ETag, conditional writes If-Match / If-None-Match), Azure Blob ETag, Microsoft Graph (eTag vs cTag: metadata vs content). Recommend: one aggregate sequence vs separate metadata validator and content validator; how collaborative (CRDT/Yjs) edits should interact with an editorial sequence/ETag (should every Yjs update bump the sequence?).

4. Collaborative editing state. For Yjs/Hocuspocus (and Google Docs / Notion / Confluence if documented): how to handle restoring an old revision while clients are connected (document "generation"/"epoch" reset so stale clients cannot merge old CRDT state back), permission downgrade to read-only during a live session, token expiry/revocation in long websocket sessions, snapshots vs updates storage, and persistence of Yjs binary state alongside a canonical JSON representation.

5. Document type / schema registry. How do ProseMirror/TipTap ecosystems, Atlassian Document Format (ADF), Notion blocks, Portable Text or Lexical handle schema versioning, migrations of stored JSON, and unknown node/mark types (safe fallback rendering vs rejection)? Recommend a registry design: type id, schema version, codecs, upgrade-on-read vs batch migration, unknown-type fallback.

6. Export. Drive files.export (formats, 10 MB limit, exportLinks), Confluence/Notion export. Authorization of export (same as read? separate "download/copy" restrictions like Drive copyRequiresWriterPermission / Box download restrictions / shared link "can download" flag).

7. API stability. How these vendors evolve APIs without breaking clients (Drive v2->v3, Box versioned endpoints, Stripe dated versions, Graph v1.0 vs beta) and which lessons apply to a PHP library following SemVer: what should be part of the stable public contract (enums, error codes, event payloads, schema), what should be extension points.

Finish with a compact table: concern | industry pattern | recommendation for my package | risk if ignored.

## r1 — deep research: агрегаты, удаление, валидаторы, коллаборация, схемы, экспорт, стабильность

Use separate file and document aggregates sharing a common node/metadata row, with immutable content revisions, copy-forward restore, and a distinct mutable collaboration state. The vendor APIs support this separation of responsibilities, but they do not disclose their internal database schemas; treating their public resource shapes as proof of a particular table design would overstate the evidence.
One important correction: Google Workspace revisions are not downloadable as raw blob revisions, but current Drive documentation does describe exporting historical Workspace revisions through revision exportLinks and through files.download long-running operations. “Google Docs revisions cannot be downloaded/exported” is therefore too broad.
Below, “documented” means public official documentation, including official SDK documentation. Recommendations are proposed package behavior, not claims about vendor internals. Where a requested mechanism is not established by the reviewed documentation, I say so explicitly.

## 1. Aggregates and revisions

Documented vendor behavior
Common pattern
The useful convergence is common identity plus specialized content behavior—not “every content type uses the same revision representation.” Box, Graph, and Confluence explicitly document copy-forward restore. Public APIs generally distinguish content identity, mutable metadata, revision retention, and current-head selection.
“Immutable revision” should mean immutable content payload and provenance. It should not mean that retention flags, publication settings, legal-hold associations, or availability can never change.
Recommendation for your package
Use something like:
```
nodes id, tenant_id, parent_id, kind, name metadata_seq, lifecycle_seq, acl_seq explicitly_trashed_at, purge_after, archived_at files node_id PK/FK current_revision_id file_revisions id, file_node_id, revision_no blob_id, size, media_type created_at, created_by, restored_from_revision_id documents node_id PK/FK type_key, generation current_revision_id editorial_seq document_revisions id, document_node_id, revision_no type_key, schema_version yjs_checkpoint_blob_id, json_projection_blob_id generation, persisted_update_seq created_at, created_by, restored_from_revision_id document_working_states document_node_id, generation checkpoint_blob_id, persisted_update_seq document_updates document_node_id, generation, update_seq, update_blob_id
```
The distinction between current_revision_id and working state is essential: a document may have a latest saved/editorial revision while connected clients are editing newer working content.
For relational integrity:
- Make subtype ownership explicit: a folder has neither file nor document content.
- Enforce that a current revision belongs to the same aggregate, preferably with a composite foreign key or equivalent database constraint.
- Keep revision_no, schema_version, and CRDT generation independent.
- Restore by inserting a new revision with restored_from_revision_id; never decrement revision numbers.
- For binary restore, reuse the existing immutable blob, not necessarily its bytes.
- For document restore, create a new collaboration generation as discussed below.
A polymorphic head pointer is defensible only if both revision types live beneath a real common revision table with enforceable ownership constraints. A Laravel morph relation pointing directly into unrelated tables buys convenience at the expense of database-enforced correctness.

## 2. Deletion, holds, and quarantine

Documented deletion behavior
OneDrive Personal and work/school OneDrive are different recovery products. The 93-day two-stage statement above is specifically the Microsoft 365 SharePoint/work-school behavior; it should not be applied indiscriminately to personal accounts.
Folder trash and restoration
Drive documents inherited trash separately from explicit trash, but the reviewed guide does not fully specify every nested restoration edge case—for example, an independently trashed descendant, subsequently trashed ancestors, and restoration into changed ownership/layout. It does establish the distinction your model needs.
For your package, define the rule explicitly:
```
effective_trashed(node) = node.explicitly_trashed_at != null OR any ancestor is explicitly trashed
```
Then restoring a parent removes its inherited effect but does not restore a child that was independently trashed. Do not overwrite every descendant’s independent trash flag during folder trash.
Also define child restoration when its original parent remains trashed or no longer exists: reject it, restore ancestors explicitly, or require an authorized fallback destination. Avoid silently moving it into a more broadly shared location.
Archive is not trash
Slack documents archive as closing a channel to new activity while retaining its history. Notion’s current help distinguishes page archive from deletion, but its older API field archived was an alias for trash; API version 2026-03-11 removed that field in favor of in_trash. That terminology collision is a particularly strong warning against copying vendor names without their versioned semantics.
The reviewed Drive and Box resource documentation does not establish a generic node-level “archive = read-only” lifecycle. Box file locks are restrictions with their own ownership/expiry semantics, not a universal archive state. Likewise, storage tiering or hiding a shared drive should not automatically be interpreted as read-only archive.
Common pattern and recommendation
Do not make this one giant enum:
```
lifecycle: active | trashed | purged editorial: writable | archived security: pending_scan | clean | quarantined | rejected preservation: retention constraints + legal holds physical_storage: present | deletion_pending | deleted
```
These dimensions overlap. A trashed, quarantined revision may still be legally held.
Recommended purge process:
- Authorize purge separately from trash.
- Calculate the effective preservation constraints over revisions and attachments.
- Make logical purge irreversible and record an audit/tombstone.
- Remove eligible references transactionally.
- Queue physical garbage collection through an outbox.
- Recheck reachability and storage-level locks before physical deletion.
- Record failures and retry; never report “bytes erased” merely because the node disappeared.
For deduplicated blobs, use reachability across current revisions, historical revisions, document attachments, pending uploads, exports, and holds. A refcount may accelerate this, but should not be your sole correctness mechanism; protect against concurrent attachment/GC races.
Vendor deduplication and internal blob-GC algorithms are not documented by the reviewed public APIs. Dropbox explicitly says deleting your copy does not delete another user’s copy, but that establishes logical independence, not a particular internal refcount implementation.
Content-addressing also creates a retention consequence: a retained reference may prevent deletion of shared physical bytes. Prefer deduplication within a tenant/security-and-retention domain, and do not claim per-node physical erasure while other references remain.
Infected content
Drive restricts abusive downloads and requires risk acknowledgment for permitted download cases. Nextcloud documents upload scanning and configurable logging versus deletion for infected files. Neither behavior establishes a universal quarantine state shared across all vendors.
For your package, quarantine should block normal download, preview, export, and collaborator access without overriding preservation. Keep scan results attributable to a scanner/signature version, and make any privileged unsafe-download path explicit and audited.

## 3. Concurrency and live collaboration

Topic 3: documented validators
The convergence is opaque equality tokens for conditional operations, with separate content identities where useful. There is no universal rule that one sequence must serve metadata, content, events, authorization, and collaborative updates.
Recommendation
Use separate internal counters/tokens but expose a convenient combined validator:
```
metadata_seq rename, move, metadata changes lifecycle_seq trash, restore, archive, purge transitions acl_seq authorization changes content_token file revision; or document generation + durable update position editorial_seq saved/published/restored document revisions
```
For a node representation containing all those fields, its ETag must change whenever any represented field changes. A metadata-only endpoint can use a metadata-scoped ETag. Return opaque quoted validators, not counters clients are encouraged to increment.
Define each command’s precondition scope:
- Rename/move: metadata/tree preconditions.
- Replace binary content: current content token.
- Restore document: current generation, durable working-state token, and authorization.
- Publish/checkpoint: expected working-state token and editorial sequence.
- Trash/purge: lifecycle and preservation checks, plus appropriate coordination with content changes.
Use database compare-and-swap or row locking for the actual decision. Reading a sequence, comparing it in PHP, and later writing without an atomic condition still loses updates.
Every Yjs update should not create an editorial revision or bump a metadata validator. Maintain a separate durable update position; advance the document’s persisted-content token when accepted changes become durable. A node ETag that claims to include current persisted content must reflect that advancement.
CRDT updates themselves should not require If-Match on the previous content token: that would defeat concurrent merging. Generation, permissions, schema compatibility, limits, and durability still require enforcement.
Topic 4: documented collaboration mechanisms
Yjs updates are binary, commutative, associative, and idempotent. mergeUpdates does not garbage-collect deleted content; loading a Y.Doc is needed for that compaction. Yjs documents disabling GC to preserve old content for historical restoration.
Hocuspocus documents:
- onAuthenticate and server-side connection readOnly.
- beforeHandleMessage rejection, including token-expiry checks.
- onTokenSync, token requests, and updating live connection permissions.
- Debounced onStoreDocument.
- JSON/HTML as projections, not primary collaboration storage.
The reviewed Google Docs, Notion, and Confluence public API documentation does not disclose their live-session CRDT/OT persistence, restore-generation protocol, or websocket revocation implementation. Confluence’s copy-forward restore does not tell us how its editor fences connected clients.
Restore recommendation: generation fencing
Generation reset is your application protocol—not a built-in Yjs guarantee documented here.
```
room = tenant_id / document_id / generation
```
Implement restore as a coordinated operation:
- Establish a restore fence and stop accepting writes for the old generation.
- Capture/flush the accepted old working state if your audit policy requires it.
- Reconstruct the chosen historical content from an independently recoverable checkpoint.
- Create a new generation and new copy-forward editorial revision.
- Commit the generation/head transition with an atomic precondition.
- Fence old hub instances and delayed persistence jobs; old-generation writes must fail at storage.
- Close old sessions and require new authorization for the new room.
- Create a fresh client Y.Doc and generation-scoped local persistence.
Do not apply a historical Yjs update to the existing live document and call that restore. Updates merge; they do not mean “replace the whole document with this earlier state.”
An old offline client must not be allowed to upload its old state into the new room. Bind tokens to tenant, document, generation, permissions, expiry, and an authorization revision. Room naming alone is not authorization.
You can seed the new generation from the historical binary checkpoint, provided old state is strictly fenced. Alternatively, intentionally reconstruct a fresh CRDT from validated historical JSON when you want to reset CRDT identity; treat that as a deliberate generation-changing conversion, not routine persistence.
Live permission and token handling
On downgrade, update server-side readOnly or disconnect and reauthenticate. On access removal, stop outbound synchronization too: rejecting edits alone still permits reading.
Use expiry checks before processing messages, a deadline timer for idle connections, revocation notifications to all hub instances, and periodic revalidation as a fallback. Current Hocuspocus documentation provides the relevant hooks, but your package must define the revocation latency and failure policy.
Do not rely on editor.setEditable(false) for authorization.
Persistence recommendation
Store authoritative Yjs binary state plus a versioned JSON projection generated from the same durable checkpoint:
```
generation persisted_update_seq yjs_checkpoint json_projection type_key schema_version projection_codec_version
```
Use append-only updates plus periodic full-state checkpoints, or another explicitly defined durable strategy. A Yjs state vector or lightweight historical snapshot is not a standalone full-content backup.
Keep editorial checkpoints independently recoverable before pruning updates. Generate JSON only from the authoritative checkpoint and record its source position. Do not allow both JSON and Yjs to be independently writable sources of truth.
Finally, debounced persistence is not a zero-loss durability promise. If clients receive synchronization success before durable storage, document the crash-loss window or add an explicit durable-save acknowledgment. Hocuspocus’s store hook supplies persistence integration; it does not remove that product-level decision.

## 4. Schemas and export

Topic 5: documented schema behavior
Typed structured content and registered codecs are common. A universal migration/version policy is not. Safe display of an unknown node and safe editing of that node are different capabilities.
Registry recommendation
Define a stable namespaced type identifier, independent of PHP class names:
```
type_key: vendor.rich_text schema_version: 4
```
Register:
```
DocumentTypeDefinition typeKey() readableVersions() writableVersion() validate() jsonCodec() collaborationCodec() renderer() exporters() migrations() clientCompatibility()
```
Recommended policies:
- Preserve original stored bytes and schema version for every historical revision.
- Make migrations deterministic, sequential, testable, and explicit about loss.
- Permit upgrade-on-read for a transient projection, without silently rewriting history.
- Use batch migration for persisted working-state changes, with auditability, rollback data, and generation fencing where necessary.
- Reject writes from clients that cannot safely round-trip the current schema.
- Render unknown types as escaped inert placeholders while retaining their original payload server-side.
- Never interpret an unknown type as arbitrary HTML or as a dynamically instantiated PHP class.
- Distinguish unsupported type, unsupported schema, corrupt payload, and prohibited content.
A fallback renderer must not become a lossy serializer. If the editor cannot preserve an unknown node, make the document read-only rather than allowing the next save to delete it.
Test migration and codec round trips, old-client writes, unknown marks, attachment references, and malicious URLs. Treat schema changes affecting Yjs content as collaboration-protocol changes, not only JSON transformations.
Topic 6: documented export behavior
Drive’s copyRequiresWriterPermission is a restriction on copying/printing/downloading for readers/commenters, not a universal “export permission equals writer” rule. Current download documentation additionally describes download-restriction metadata, so calculate effective capabilities rather than relying on one legacy-looking field.
Export is a rendition of authorized content, not necessarily identical to read access or to the source format.
Define separate policy abilities for:
```
view_metadata view_content download_original export_document copy_node read_history export_history
```
Hosts may map export_document to view_content by default, but the extension point should permit stricter policy.
An export request should pin:
```
document revision/checkpoint format exporter version options attachment reference set
```
Generate larger exports asynchronously. Recheck authorization when issuing and redeeming download access; a successful queued job must not grant permanent access after revocation. Include referenced attachments only when authorized.
Cache exports by immutable source checkpoint plus exporter/options—not by node ID alone. Keep rendition blobs distinct from original content and give them their own expiration policy.
Do not copy Drive’s 10 MB limit unless you want that product constraint. Also do not claim lossless export when the target cannot represent your nodes; report omitted/approximated content.

## 5. Stability and decision table

Topic 7: documented API evolution
Mature systems distinguish transport/API version, serialized content format, SDK/library version, and stored-data migration. They are not one interchangeable version number.
Recommendation for a SemVer PHP package
Declare the stable public contract explicitly:
- Supported service interfaces, commands, DTOs, and documented method signatures.
- Node kinds, lifecycle transitions, restore semantics, revision ownership, and concurrency preconditions.
- Public error codes and their meanings, including retryability—not exception prose.
- Document type identifiers, schema envelopes, migration guarantees, and supported codec versions.
- Public domain-event payloads and their ordering/delivery promises.
- Authorization abilities and the behavior of policy extension points.
- Documented configuration keys and installation/migration guarantees.
Good stable errors include precondition_failed, generation_mismatch, unsupported_schema, retention_blocked, legal_hold_blocked, and content_quarantined. Include structured context while avoiding accidental information disclosure.
Keep extension points narrow:
```
BlobStore DocumentTypeRegistry DocumentCodec ExportRenderer AuthorizationResolver RetentionPolicyResolver MalwareScanner CollaborationGateway
```
Do not make raw Eloquent serialization, storage paths, table layout, Hocuspocus hook payloads, or vendor response objects your default public contract. However, if you explicitly support host applications querying or extending package tables/models, those documented relationships and columns become a compatibility obligation.
For public events, use a versioned envelope:
```
{ "event_id": "opaque-id", "event_type": "document.revision_created", "event_version": 1, "tenant_id": "opaque-id", "aggregate_id": "opaque-id", "aggregate_seq": 42, "occurred_at": "2026-10-07T12:00:00Z", "payload": { "revision_id": "opaque-id", "restored_from_revision_id": null } }
```
Specify at-least-once delivery if that is your actual guarantee; consumers should deduplicate by event_id. Do not expose a sequence called “all changes” if it intentionally excludes working CRDT updates.
Be careful with enum evolution: adding a value can break exhaustive PHP match consumers even if adding an optional JSON field would not. Declare whether a vocabulary is closed or extensible, and require unknown-value handling for extensible wire contracts.
Database upgrades should use expand/migrate/contract phases where mixed package/hub versions may coexist. Never require old revisions to be destructively rewritten merely to load them under a new release.
Compact decision table

## r2 — Hocuspocus persistence (обрезан)

Use persisted Yjs binary as the authoritative state, load it before synchronization, and treat JSON as a projection or a one-time import. For a hard restore that replaces CRDT history, use a new generation in the room identity, reject old-generation writes in Laravel, and rebuild each client’s Y.Doc; merely replacing a database blob and disconnecting clients is not sufficient.
Below I distinguish documented behavior from architectural recommendations. Important verification limitation: the official documentation and v4 release notes were retrievable, but the GitHub source-file bodies were not. Consequently, I cannot honestly claim a line-by-line audit of sync-message enforcement or unloadDocument guards for every v3/v4 patch release.

## r3 — Hocuspocus v4 hooks, fence, readOnly, transformer

Use binary Yjs state as the authoritative storage; seed JSON once on the server, enforce permissions there, and treat document eviction as separate from persistence cancellation. The answers below use current v4 documentation—not old v2/v3 snippets.

## (a) Loading and initial content

The hook is an async function receiving one payload object:
```
async onLoadDocument({ document, documentName, context, instance, requestHeaders, requestParameters, socketId, }) { const state = await loadBinary(documentName) if (state) { Y.applyUpdate(document, state) // Uint8Array; Node Buffer also works } }
```
You can mutate the supplied document as above, return a Y.Doc, or—in v4—return a raw Uint8Array update directly. requestHeaders is a web-standard Headers object. See .
Seed initial content in this server-side loading path, once per logical document. Independently converting the same JSON on every client creates separate Yjs insertions with different CRDT identities; synchronization merges those insertions rather than recognizing them as “the same initial content,” producing duplicates. Client content/setContent(JSON) is therefore not a substitute for loading collaborative state. The official persistence guide explicitly warns that recreating Yjs state from JSON on connections causes duplication; persist Y.encodeStateAsUpdate(document) instead.
With multiple servers, “once” must also be enforced atomically in shared storage—not merely by checking that the local document is empty.

## (b) Disconnect, unload, suppress storage

For the built-in v4 Server, access the collaboration instance through server.hocuspocus:
```
const hp = server.hocuspocus hp.closeConnections(documentName)
```
This closes that document’s connections on the local instance; it does not mean “cancel persistence.” See . v4 deliberately retains/retries documents when storage fails, and shutdown flushes pending stores.
Important distinctions:
- unloadDocument takes the managed Document object, not just its name. However, the current official public methods page does not document it as a supported eviction API; verify its guards/signature against your pinned v4 patch before relying on it. Old declarations found online are not sufficient evidence for v4.
- Calling document.destroy() directly is not equivalent to managed unloading: the documented unloading lifecycle includes destruction and afterUnloadDocument, which extensions can use for cleanup. Do not substitute raw Yjs destruction for that lifecycle.
- No documented public “close and discard all pending stores” operation appears in those official pages. Do not assume disconnect or destroy cancels a debounce.
For deletion/reset, the reliable application-level solution is a storage fence:
- Atomically mark the record deleted, or increment its generation, and reject new connections.
- Make every persistence writer conditionally write only when the record is active and its generation matches the generation loaded with that document.
- Close connections on every instance, then let managed unloading finish.
For example, make the write conditional on WHERE id = ? AND generation = ? AND deleted_at IS NULL. That also rejects an already-running stale store, which canceling a timer cannot stop. This is a backend design recommendation, not a Hocuspocus cancellation API. All persistence extensions must obey the fence; a guard in a later hook cannot undo an earlier database write. Hooks execute sequentially through extensions and configuration.

## (c) Read-only and revalidation

Yes: connection.readOnly = true is server-side enforcement, not merely an editor UI setting. The official authentication example says such changes are not accepted or synchronized to other clients. See and . This does not prohibit your own server-side mutations.
- beforeHandleMessage: runs before handling/applying an incoming message. Check expiry/revocation from trusted context or your permission service; throw to reject the message and close the connection. It is the documented place for enforcement before application—not onChange, which runs afterward.
- onTokenSync: revalidate a token during an existing connection and update the live connection.readOnly. The provider can call provider.sendToken(); the server can ask via connection.requestToken(). It is event-driven, not an automatic expiry timer, so token synchronization alone is insufficient if a client never sends another token. See .

## (d) Transformer and fragment name

Yes—for one-time import/migration or initial seeding, the official docs recommend @hocuspocus/transformer for Tiptap-compatible ProseMirror

## r4 — корзина, восстановление, контейнеры

The key distinction is inherited deletion versus independent deletion: restoring a container should not undo an earlier, separate deletion of a child. These vendors do not expose one universal lifecycle model; owner deletion, asynchronous work, and name conflicts are endpoint-specific.

## 1. Google Drive trash semantics

Official documentation: , .
Example: trash child A, then trash its parent containing A and B. Restoring the parent restores B’s inherited state; A remains independently trashed.
Parent still trashed or permanently deleted: the cited v3 documentation does not specify a complete contract for whether an individual restore reparents the item, restores ancestors, fails, or leaves an inherited trash state. Do not promise automatic ancestor restoration or root fallback. Verify the returned parents, trashed, and explicitlyTrashed, and explicitly select a live destination when your application requires predictable placement. Also, permanent deletion of a folder deletes its user-owned descendants, so a surviving restorable child cannot be assumed.

## 2. Box restoration and retention

Official references: , , .
- Restore with POST /files/{id} or POST /folders/{id}. Supply parent: {"id":"..."} if the original parent no longer exists. Important: the file reference explicitly says this is a fallback only—it is used only when the original folder no longer exists, not an unconditional relocation parameter.
- A same-name destination item produces 409; restore accepts an optional new name. There is no documented automatic suffix policy for these restore endpoints.
- Default trash retention is 30 days; business/enterprise administrators can shorten or lengthen it. Retention policies and legal holds can prevent permanent deletion. Paying customers may have a further 14-day support recovery grace period after purge—not an ordinary API restore window.
- Restoring a parent does not restore sub-items deleted before the parent was deleted.

## Что принято, что отложено, что отклонено

Принято: раздельные агрегаты File/Document на общем узле (уже OPUS D16); неизменяемые ревизии + copy-forward restore с restored_from_revision_id (D34); отдельное рабочее состояние документа (D34); голова агрегата принадлежит тому же агрегату — составной FK (D34); раздельные валидаторы узла и содержимого, CRDT без If-Match (D35); серверная загрузка состояния хабом, JSON — проекция, одноразовое серверное сидирование через transformer, поколение в имени комнаты, storage fence по epoch, readOnly на сервере, beforeHandleMessage для истечения токена (D36); явные корни корзины и запрет тихого переноса в корень (D37); archive — обратимое read-only состояние контейнера (D37); delete_with_owner по умолчанию false (OPUS D27 + Google Workspace); экспорт — отдельная абилити Download, привязан к неизменяемой ревизии, кэш только по (ревизия, экспортёр, формат) (P4.4); неизвестный тип/непредставимый контент — read-only, не lossy save (P4.3); стабильные коды ошибок и объявление закрытых/расширяемых enum (P4 rules).
Отложено (T2, вне 1.0, AD39-стиль): retention policies/legal holds, асинхронные экспорты больших документов, append-only журнал Yjs-обновлений (используется компактный state + checkpoint'ы), мгновенный разрыв по отзыву прав для всех инстансов (используется проверка на authenticate/store/beforeHandleMessage по exp, OPUS D24), раздельные metadata/lifecycle/acl счётчики (одна node.sequence достаточна для 1.0).
Отклонено: полиморфный указатель головы (N03), архив как алиас корзины (Notion API 2026-03-11 урок), лимит 10 МБ Drive как продуктовое ограничение (лимит — конфиг documents.max_content_size).
